author: Mo Qureshi
headline: Saudi construction drives Gulf decorative coatings demand
deck: Decorative and construction coatings follow the build programme with a lag, and the Gulf's is arriving now.
excerpt: Decorative and construction coatings demand follows a building programme by two to three years, which places the Gulf's peak coatings demand in the current window.
content:
The Middle East Coatings Show runs at Expo City in Dubai at the end of September, and while its exhibitor profile is weighted toward industrial raw materials, the demand behind the regional market is substantially a construction story.

Coatings demand lags construction activity by a predictable interval. Paint goes on near the end of a building programme, after the structure is complete and the interior fit-out is under way, which places peak coatings demand two to three years behind peak concrete. Saudi Arabia's construction programme, running through the giga-projects and the residential build-out this publication has tracked, therefore generates a coatings requirement that is arriving now rather than at the point contracts were awarded.

Volume is only part of it. The specification mix in the Saudi programme skews toward performance categories rather than standard decorative product, for reasons connected to how the buildings are being procured. Hotel and hospitality construction under international operator brand standards, which this publication has covered in the context of a hotel pipeline near 99,500 rooms, brings specification requirements on washability, durability and low emissions that a domestic residential specification would not impose. Institutional and cultural buildings carry fire performance requirements. External facades in the Gulf climate require ultraviolet and thermal cycling resistance well beyond a temperate-market product.

That mix favours suppliers with technical service capability rather than those competing purely on price. Specification selling — persuading an architect or a project's technical team to write a product into the documents — is the mechanism by which construction coatings are won, and it happens years before the order.

Regional manufacturers have positioned accordingly. This publication has reported CMCI putting four decades of Saudi-made construction chemicals on the Big 5 floor, Arkaz exhibiting months after the Master Builders deal closed, and Henkel Polybit bringing its Gulf waterproofing portfolio to Riyadh. Jotun and Henkel Polybit both appear among the attending partners at the Saudi Mega Projects conference in Riyadh in the same week as this show, which is the demand side of the same business.

Waterproofing deserves separate mention because it is where coating failure is most expensive. A failed external coating is an appearance problem addressed at the next maintenance cycle; a failed waterproofing membrane below grade or on a roof is a building fabric problem requiring destructive access to repair.

Exhibitor and sponsor detail is taken from the organiser's published material. Specification is also where a coating supplier's technical service earns its margin, long before any order is placed. Waterproofing failures also surface years after handover, which places them awkwardly between defect liability and operational maintenance.
